summary.text: Eunomia is the personification of good order and obedience to just law — one of the three Horae whom Themis bore to Zeus, alongside her sisters Dike (Justice) and Eirene (Peace).
She embodies the well-governed city and stands as the exact moral counterpart of Dysnomia (Lawlessness), the fatherless child of Eris.

story.text: After Zeus swallowed Metis and made Athena his own, he took bright Themis as his wife, and she bore the Horae — Eunomia (Order), Dike (Justice) and blooming Eirene (Peace) — 'who mind the works of mortal men,' together with the Moirai whom Zeus honored above all. Eunomia is thus a goddess of the second divine generation, born of a Titan mother and the king of the gods, her domain set squarely within the affairs of humankind.

Her name carries her nature: eunomia is the Greek ideal of good government, the condition of a city whose citizens keep just law and right custom. She personifies the well-ordered polis itself — lawful conduct, civic harmony and the obedience that lets a community flourish. As one of the Horae she works in concert with her sisters, so that justice (Dike) and peace (Eirene) attend wherever good order is kept.

Hesiod sets Eunomia in deliberate opposition to Dysnomia, Lawlessness, whom Eris (Strife) bore without a father among her brood of grim children. The two are moral poles of the same cosmos: where Eunomia upholds the well-governed city, Dysnomia unmakes it, so that the breakdown of law is figured as the dark mirror of the order Eunomia maintains.

Hyginus likewise makes Eunomia a daughter of Jove (Zeus) and Themis and numbers her among the Horae beside Dike and Eirene; but he gives an expanded catalogue of the Hours — Auco, Eunomia, Pherusa, Carpo, Dike, Euporia, Eirene, Orthosie and Thallo — rather than Hesiod's canonical three, reflecting the later mythographers' larger and divergent lists.
